frameworks.name: Scaling Roadmap Stages
frameworks.definition: A 10-stage growth model documenting the predictable progression, stall points, and breakthrough solutions across product, marketing, sales, customer success, recruiting, IT, HR, and finance functions.

claims.text: To earn money at a given scale, one must endure an equivalent quantity of pain: earning $1M requires enduring $1M worth of pain; earning $10M requires enduring $10M worth of pain. The nature of pain changes by stage (early stage: not knowing; mid-stage: judgment from others; mature: lawsuits and ambiguity), but the constancy of pain never resolves.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Outcomes are directly proportional to accumulated sacrifices; the pain is not avoidable but rather shifts in form as the business matures.

numbers.axis: Revenue target vs. pain endured (proportional relationship)

bounded_by: The pain is unavoidable regardless of scale; attempting to eliminate it is futile

claims.text: Big goals and small goals require roughly equivalent effort and pain: building a highly successful local restaurant (80-hour weeks, complex team management) and building a billion-dollar unicorn (same management complexity) both require sustained hard work. Since effort is constant regardless of scale, one should pursue larger goals.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: When choosing between goal sizes of different scales
claims.mechanism: Effort required scales linearly with ambition, so the comparative pain-per-unit-outcome favors larger goals; small goals do not reduce suffering but limit upside.

claims.text: Suffering is a constant across all growth states: if growing, in pain; if plateaued, in pain; if declining, in pain. Therefore, pain should not be a decision criterion; it is simply always present and should be treated as background noise rather than a signal.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: In any operating business across all stages
claims.mechanism: Pain is a constant function of ambition and growth, not a variable outcome; treating it as a signal (rather than context) causes decision-making to be paralyzed by false urgency.

claims.text: Competition for big goals is thinner because most people judge large goals as unrealistic and do not pursue them, resulting in fewer competitors at the highest ambition levels than at local/small-business levels.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: In goal selection and market entry
claims.mechanism: Psychological barrier (perception of unrealism) creates competitive moat; fewer people enter because of false belief, not actual difficulty.
bounded_by: Does not apply to markets with regulatory barriers or genuine capital constraints

claims.text: Most problems are solvable, and most things are knowable. The reason someone has not reached their goal is not lack of knowledge availability but lack of obsessive pursuit and trial initiation.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: In business and personal goal achievement
claims.mechanism: Knowledge is discoverable through obsessive iteration; the bottleneck is initiation and persistence, not information access.

claims.text: If pursuing extraordinary outcomes, it is normal and necessary to operate differently from one's normal peer group. Divergence from normal peer behavior is a positive indicator (green flag) that you are building a different life trajectory than your friends.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: When comparing lifestyle and behavior choices to a reference peer group without equivalent ambition
claims.mechanism: Identical behavior produces identical outcomes; divergence from peer norm is mathematically necessary to diverge from peer outcomes; unusualness signals directional correctness rather than error.
bounded_by: Does not apply to divergence toward destructive or illegal behavior

examples.text: Hormozi recounts a conversation with his executive assistants where they observed his lifestyle and car choices, remarking that if he were a normal person, he would drive a different car. He pointed out the logical tautology: 'If I were not me, I would do things that not-me would do.' This illustrates that behaving like normal people while expecting extraordinary outcomes is contradictory; divergence is necessary.

Hormozi references Stephen Schwartzman (founder of Blackstone) as the source of the insight that big goals and small goals require equivalent effort. Both involve managing teams, extended work hours, and coordination complexity; the difference is scale of outcome, not effort per se.

practices.text: Place your business information into the $100 million scaling roadmap quiz at acquisition.com/roadmap to identify your growth stage and the critical function (product, marketing, sales, customer success, recruiting, IT, HR, finance) to optimize next.
Book a call with Hormozi's team via the roadmap tool's thank-you page to have your business evaluated; if they can help scale it, they will invite you to an in-person workshop in Vegas.
